title: Cold open: the boy who read this book
cues: Corsica, 1780s: candlelight; a boy's hands turning old pages (point of view); then wider, the room; a Napoleon engraving.
Title: *Plutarch's Lives*, then *Alexander*.

lines.text: Long before he was an emperor, a quiet boy from Corsica spent his evenings with one book.
It held the lives of ancient men: generals, lawgivers, kings. His name was Napoleon Bonaparte.
The book was Plutarch's Lives.
Before he ever commanded an army, he was shaped by stories. Every page quietly answered a question for him:
what does a great man do?
Tonight, you're going to read the same book. Not as a spectator.
As him.

title: 1. A writer who cared about small things
cues: Plutarch's bust; a lamp; a scroll.

lines.text: Plutarch lived about four hundred years after Alexander, and before he begins, he warns us.
He isn't writing history. He's writing lives.
A famous battle, he says, often tells you less about a man than a small remark, or how he treats someone who has no power over him.
So tonight, don't just watch what happens. Watch the small choices. They're the ones the Observer remembers.

title: 2. Born into a story
cues: Mountains of Macedonia at dawn; the palace at Pella; a lion seal; the temple of Artemis burning far away.

lines.text: Alexander was born in Macedonia, son of King Philip and Queen Olympias.
People told strange stories about his birth.
His mother dreamed a thunderbolt struck her.
His father dreamed of a lion.
On the day he was born, it was said, the great temple at Ephesus burned.
Plutarch doesn't swear any of it is true. But the boy grew up hearing it.
Before he'd done a single thing, he was told he was special.
That's a belief handed to a child before there's any evidence. Maybe someone said something like that to you.
You're the smart one. You're the strong one. Or maybe they said the opposite.
Either way, you've been carrying it longer than you remember.

title: 3. A boy who asked the right questions
cues: Point of view: a boy's view up at tall Persian envoys in silk; a map of roads unrolling on a table.

lines.text: As a boy he wanted honour, but only the real kind.
Asked if he'd race at the Olympic Games, he said yes, if the other runners were kings.
When envoys came from the king of Persia, he didn't ask them about gold.
He asked how long the roads were. How their king fought. How big his army was.
And whenever news came of another of his father's victories, he'd complain to his friends:
My father will leave me nothing great to do.
That's the need to matter: significance. It forms early, often in the shadow of someone bigger.
A little brother racing the older one. A son measuring himself against his father's trophies.
It can make you great. Keep watching. It can also break you.

title: 4. The horse (IMMERSE)
cues: Point of view. Dust in low gold light; a black stallion rearing close; men stepping back; your own small hands open in front of you; the sun ahead; the horse's shadow stretching across the ground. Close sound: hooves, snorting, breath.
Silence. Three seconds. The horse breathing.
Beat. Then the move.
The gold dot lands on the shadow behind the horse.

lines.text: You are twelve years old. The air smells of dust and sweat and leather.
In front of you, a black horse is screaming and rearing, higher than the men around him.
They call him Bucephalus.
Your father's best riders have tried him, one after another, and every one has been thrown or has backed away.
Your father is tired of it. He tells them to take the horse away.
And the men nod, because that's what you do when the king has decided.
But you've been watching. Not the horse's hooves. His eyes. Every time he lunges, he's jumping away from something on the ground.
His own shadow, black and moving at his feet.
The men are laughing at you for speaking up. Your father is watching to see if you'll embarrass him.
Your heart is pounding.
What do you do?
You walk forward, slowly.
You take the reins and turn his head toward the sun, so the shadow falls behind him, where he can't see it.
You speak low. You put your hand on his neck and feel him trembling under your palm.
Then, in one motion, you're on his back. And you let him run.
When you ride back, your father has tears in his eyes. My son, he says, find a kingdom big enough for you.
Macedonia is too small.
Feel what just happened inside you. Not the applause. Something quieter.
A part of you watched you see what the grown men missed, and it wrote it down:
I see what others miss. I move when others give up. That's the Observer.
It doesn't believe what you say about yourself. It believes what it sees you do.
You've had moments like this. Fixing what the adults gave up on.
Finishing the rep when everyone else racked the weight. Nobody throws a party.
But a belief is born.
What's the last thing you did that gave your Observer real evidence?

title: 5. The book under the pillow (IMMERSE)
cues: Night in Mieza: the window glowing blue; a small wooden box; your hand sliding the *Iliad* under a pillow beside a dagger; candle smoke.

lines.text: Your father sends for the wisest man in Greece to teach you:
Aristotle. In a quiet grove you learn about the stars and the body and justice and poetry.
And at night, alone in your room, you open the one book you love more than any other:
the story of Achilles, the greatest warrior who ever lived. You read until the candle gutters.
Then you slide the book under your pillow, next to your dagger, and you lie down on both of them.
In the dark, you can feel the edge of the book through the pillow.
And you think, the way boys do: one day, they'll tell stories about me.
A book and a blade under the same pillow. This is the whole idea of tonight.
The stories you fall asleep with become the person you try to be.
His was Achilles. For you, maybe it was a show, a poster above the bed, a voice in your earbuds.
You didn't choose those beliefs. You absorbed them, night after night.
What did you fall asleep next to?
And is it the person you want to become?

title: 6. A king at twenty
cues: The theatre; a sudden blade; your father falling; the crowd turning to look at *you*. Map: rebellions everywhere.

lines.text: You are twenty. Your father is murdered in front of a crowd by one of his own guards.
And in that moment, every face turns toward you. Cities rebel. Advisers tell you to wait, to go carefully.
Stop here. Underneath everything in this second runs one question. It's the question your Observer asks in every room you walk into:
who are we, here?
Until it has an answer, you don't know how to stand, how to speak, what to do with your hands.
Yesterday the answer was the king's son. Now the role has landed on you.
But a role isn't a belief. The Observer has to believe it, so it reaches for evidence.
A mother who told you since you were small that your birth was divine.
A father who said Macedonia was too small for you.
A horse no grown man could ride.
Years of carrying yourself like a king before anyone called you one.
The Observer looks at all of it and answers: we are the king.
And from that answer everything follows: the voice, the speed, the decisions.
You do this too. Walk into a job interview, and the room tells your Observer who you are:
the one asking. So you sit a little smaller. You speak a little softer.
You'd never take your shirt off like a lifeguard on the beach, because that person can't exist in this room.
Who you think you are and where you are have to agree.
But notice: the interview self is rented. It belongs to that room and those people; walk out, and it's gone.
The real question is what's left when the room is empty. Who are you when no one has told you?
Back in Macedonia, the advisers are still telling you to wait. Alexander did the opposite.
He moved so fast his enemies couldn't organise.
When Thebes rebelled, he destroyed it, a cruelty Plutarch says he regretted for the rest of his life.
But no one called him a boy again.

title: 7. The man in the barrel (IMMERSE)
cues: Corinth, bright sun; over your shoulder, a crowd of nobles bowing; then the street; an old man lying beside a clay jar; your shadow falls across his face.
Silence. Your friends laughing behind you.

lines.text: In Corinth, everyone who matters comes to congratulate you. Generals, statesmen, philosophers.
They bow. They smile. They want something.
Except one man. Diogenes, who owns almost nothing and sleeps in a clay jar, didn't come.
So you go to him.
You find him stretched out in the sun.
You stand over him, the most powerful young man in Greece, and you ask him:
Is there anything I can do for you?
Yes. Move. You're blocking my sun.
Your friends laugh at him. You could too. Or you could feel insulted.
Instead, you feel something you didn't expect: respect. And you say: If I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes.
Look at what he asked for. The most powerful man alive offers him anything.
He doesn't reach back to his past, the home he lost, the wealth he never had.
He doesn't reach forward to what he might need next year.
He asks for the one thing standing between him and this moment.
The sun.
Live in the past, and regret grows into depression. Live in the future, and worry grows into anxiety.
The present is the only place you can act. What you do in it becomes your future, and then your past.
Even scripture says it: don't worry about tomorrow; today has enough of its own.
Alexander wanted the whole world. Diogenes wanted nothing he didn't already have.
And Alexander saw it: a man who had conquered wanting.
That's the difference between identity and ego. Ego needs the room to clap.
Identity can stand in front of a man who wants nothing from it, and admire him.
It's looking at someone quietly fishing at the pier, needing no one's approval, and realising you envy his peace.
Only someone secure in who they are can feel that without feeling small.
Who in your life can't be impressed by you?
How do you feel around them?

title: 8. The river
cues: Over your shoulder: the river Granicus; Persian cavalry on the far bank; then underwater roar; a blade above you; a hand cutting it down.

lines.text: You're twenty-two, and you've crossed into Asia with an army. At the river Granicus, the enemy waits on the far bank.
Your generals say it's too late in the day, the water too deep.
You ride in anyway.
In the chaos, a Persian rider raises his blade over your head, and you don't see it.
A hand cuts him down. It belongs to Cleitus, one of your officers.
He just saved your life. Remember his face.

title: 9. The cup (IMMERSE)
cues: A tent at Tarsus; fever-light; your hand holding a folded letter; then a cup of medicine, close; the physician's face as he reads.
Silence. The cup, close.

lines.text: You swam in an icy river, and now you're burning with fever.
Your doctors are afraid to treat you; if you die, they'll be blamed.
Only one, Philip, offers to prepare a strong medicine.
Then a letter arrives from one of your generals. You unfold it.
Philip has been paid by the Persians to poison you.
The tent flap opens. Philip walks in with the cup.
What do you do?
You hand him the letter.
And while his eyes move across the accusation, you lift the cup and drink it all, looking straight at him.
You get well.
That's trust chosen from strength. When you know who you are, you don't have to suspect everyone to feel safe.
It's handing someone the keys and actually letting them drive. A fragile ego can't do that.
It's too busy guarding the mask.

title: 10. The tent (IMMERSE)
cues: Issus: the abandoned chariot of Darius; then your hand pulling back a tent curtain; inside, a mother, a wife, daughters, kneeling in fear; candlelight.
Silence. Your hand on the curtain.

lines.text: You've beaten Darius, the king of Persia. He fled the battlefield and left everything behind:
his chariot, his bow, his family.
Now you stand outside a tent. Inside are his mother, his wife and his daughters.
You can hear them weeping. They think they belong to you now.
In this age, they do. Whatever you decide, no one will stop you.
No one will even judge you.
What do you do?
You send word that they are safe. They keep their titles, their servants, their honour.
No one is allowed to dishonour them.
And you don't even allow yourself to look at the queen in a way that would shame her.
This is the centre of everything. Who are you when you could get away with anything?
The Observer is always watching, even when no one else is. Especially then.
It's the password no one knows you have. The money no one would miss.
The person who can't fight back. That's where identity is really built.
Not in front of the crowd. In front of God, and yourself.
When was the last time you did the right thing knowing no one would ever find out?

title: 11. One letter
cues: The desert to Siwa; heat shimmer; a temple gate; a priest's mouth forming a word.

lines.text: Alexander took the island city of Tyre, entered Egypt, and crossed the desert to the oracle at Siwa.
The priest greeted him as son of Zeus.
Some said the priest, struggling with Greek, only meant my son, and a slip of one letter changed it.
Alexander liked the second version better.
One letter, and a new identity.
Someone says the right thing about you at the right moment, and you carry it for life.
Sometimes it lifts you. Sometimes it's a mask you'll spend years trying to live up to.

title: 12. The night before (IMMERSE)
cues: Gaugamela at night: a hill; your view over a valley of endless Persian campfires; Parmenio's voice behind you; then your tent; your eyes closing.
Silence. Wind. Distant fires crackling.

lines.text: It's the night before the battle that will decide everything. You stand on a hill and look down at the plain.
Persian campfires, more than you can count, all the way to the horizon.
Your oldest general, Parmenio, comes to you.
Attack them now, in the dark. They'll never see us coming.
It would work. It might save thousands of your men.
What do you do?
You say: I will not steal my victory. And you go to sleep.
So deeply that at dawn your generals have to shake you awake.
When they ask how you could sleep, you tell them: We've already won.
He's finally stopped running.
That day, the Persian army broke. Darius was later murdered by his own men.
When Alexander found the body, he took off his cloak and laid it over him.
Fear cuts corners. Identity sleeps.
When you know who you are, you'd rather win in the open than wake up next to a victory you'd be ashamed of.

title: 13. The mask grows
cues: Babylon: gold, silk, incense; courtiers dropping to the floor before you; your sleeves now Persian silk; one philosopher standing upright, the only head not bowed.

lines.text: Now the whole Persian empire is yours. The rooms are gold. The air smells of incense.
Everywhere you go, people drop to the floor. They tell you you're more than a man.
That whatever you do is right. It feels good. Then it feels normal.
You begin to wear Persian robes. You expect people to bow. A philosopher named Callisthenes refuses.
You don't forgive him.
Notice how slowly it happens. Nobody wakes up one morning arrogant.
The applause just gets a little louder than the evidence, day after day, until you can't hear anything else.

title: 14. The banquet (IMMERSE)
cues: Torchlight; wine; laughter; the faces of flatterers close and warm; one face hard: Cleitus. A spear on the wall behind you. Then silence and darkness.
The gold dot fades out. Silence.
Long silence. Only wind.

lines.text: You're at a banquet, deep in wine. The room is warm, loud and golden.
Your new friends are praising you, above your father, above the old soldiers who bled beside you.
Then one voice cuts through. Cleitus. The man who saved your life at the river.
He stands, red-faced, and tells the room you owe everything to Macedonian blood.
This is the hand that saved you.
Everyone is looking at you. The wine is loud in your head.
There's a spear on the wall behind you.
And this time, you don't pause to choose.
You kill him.
When you understand what you've done, you collapse. For three days you lie in your tent, refusing food, calling his name.
A philosopher comes and tells you that whatever a king does must be just.
And you let yourself believe him.
This is what it looks like when ego takes over. The flatterers became the mirror.
They didn't show you what you did. They showed you what they needed you to believe.
And the one man who still told you the truth, you destroyed.
It happens quietly today, too. When the likes start deciding who you are.
When everyone around you agrees because they need something from you. The Observer stops seeing evidence, and starts hearing applause.
Who in your life tells you the truth?
When did you last thank them?

title: 15. The water (IMMERSE)
cues: India: elephants in a storm; King Porus, huge and wounded; then a white-hot desert; your cracked hands; a helmet held up to you, water catching the sun; your men's faces watching. The gold dot returns.
Silence. The helmet, close.

lines.text: You push on to India. At the river Hydaspes, you defeat King Porus, a giant who fights on even with his wounds.
You ask him how he wishes to be treated.
Like a king.
And you give him back his kingdom, and more.
Old Bucephalus dies there, the horse from your boyhood. You build a city and give it his name.
Your men are exhausted. At the next river, they refuse to go on.
You shut yourself in your tent in fury. But in the end, you turn the army home.
The way back crosses a desert that kills men by the hundred.
Your lips are split. Your tongue feels like leather.
A few soldiers have found a little water and bring it to you in a helmet.
It's cold. It shines. Everyone is watching you. Every one of them is just as thirsty.
What do you do?
You thank them. And in front of your whole army, you pour it out onto the sand.
Plutarch says it was as if every man had drunk.
Even after everything, the old identity was still there under the mask.
The boy who turned the horse toward the sun. That's the thing about identity built by action:
it can be buried, but it doesn't disappear. It waits for you to act like yourself again.

title: 16. Babylon
cues: Dusk over Babylon; a fever; a long line of soldiers filing past a bed; a raised hand. Slow, quiet.

lines.text: Back in Babylon, there are feasts, and omens, and then a fever that grows worse every day.
When your soldiers hear you're dying, they demand to see you. They walk past your bed one by one.
You can't speak anymore. You lift your hand to each of them.
Alexander died at thirty-two. Some said he was poisoned. Plutarch thought most of those stories were invented.

title: 17. Your turn
cues: The gold dot travels back through every moment: the shadow, the book, the cup, the tent, the fires, the water. Then darkness and a single candle.

lines.text: In twelve years, a young man crossed the known world. But Plutarch didn't write his life to show how far he went.
He wrote it so you could see who he was. And maybe see yourself.
So here's what you lived tonight.
Your beliefs were handed to you before you could choose them. Thunder at his birth, a book under his pillow.
For you, a show, a parent, a feed. You can't change what you absorbed.
You can choose what you feed yourself from now on.
Identity is built from evidence, and the evidence that counts most is private.
The horse. The cup. The tent. Choices made where applause didn't matter.
Ego is borrowed, and the lender always wants something back.
When the flatterers told him who he was, he lost the man who saved his life.
So, as you drift off, ask the Observer one quiet question. What did you see me do today?
Not what people said about you. What you did. And tomorrow, give it one more piece of evidence.
That was the life of Alexander. Sleep well.

title: Prologue
cues: Darkness. One candle. Slow plates: a sleeper by candlelight; an eye; Napoleon; Alexander; the book under the pillow.

lines.text: Before we begin, you should know why this was made. It isn't entertainment.
It's an investment. In you.
Everything you do comes from what you believe about yourself. Not what you say you believe.
What a quieter part of you believes. Call it the Observer. It watches everything you do, and it keeps the record.
It doesn't listen to your words. It believes your actions.
From that record, it answers one question, in every room you walk into:
who are we, here?
Whatever it answers, you become. Your voice, your posture, your decisions follow.
There's a second voice: the ego. It's the identity you borrow from other people, from the way you think they see you.
It feels real, but it's rented. It changes with the room. Walk out, and it's gone.
Identity is different. It's built from evidence. And the strongest evidence is gathered where no one is watching.
Only in front of God, and yourself.
So why stories?
Why Alexander, and Napoleon?
Because before Napoleon ever led an army, he spent his nights reading about men like Alexander.
And Alexander slept with the story of Achilles under his pillow.
The greatest people who ever lived were shaped by the stories they let in.
And when you let them in matters. As you drift toward sleep, your brain slows down.
The guarded, busy waking mind gives way to slower waves. First alpha.
Then theta, the borderland of dreams. Here, pictures come easily, and the mind is open.
Your brain uses much of the same machinery to imagine an action as it does to perform it.
So tonight, you won't just hear what they did. You'll stand where they stood.
You'll make their choices. And somewhere in the night, the Observer files a quiet note:
we have been here before. We know how this is done.
That isn't the whole work. A belief becomes who you are only when you act on it, again and again.
But this is the first step. The picture. The spark. The first impulse to move.
So get comfortable. Let your breathing slow. And listen. Not as a spectator.
As them.
